title: Rotating Capacitive System for Measurement of a Third Order Gravity Gradient Based on a Single-Axis Mechanical Oscillator. Part I, Theory
abstract: This paper is a feasibility study on a single-axis mechanical oscillator, mounted on a miniature circular rotating platform, that is proposed to be used for measuring a quantity proportional to the second vertical derivative of gravitational acceleration projected onto the oscillator's sensitivity axis. The latter is aligned with the axis of rotation. Part I establishes theoretical feasibility only. Design constraints, quantitative sensitivity, error budgets, and mobile platform performance will be addressed in Part II.

title: Quality Control for the LGAD sensors of the ATLAS High Granularity Timing Detector
authors: P. J. Dos Santos De Assis
abstract: The High Granularity Timing Detector (HGTD) currently in the production phase will mainly mitigate the pile-up effect in the ATLAS forward region and serve for bunch-by-bunch luminosity measurements in the high-luminosity (HL) phase of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The HGTD utilizes Low Gain Avalanche Detector (LGAD) technology, covering the pseudorapidity range between 2.4 and 4.0, and provides high-precision timing information to distinguish collisions occurring close in space but well-separated in time. A pre-production batch of 8-inch silicon wafers was fabricated and a systematic quality control test campaign was carried out. This paper describes the Quality Control (QC) required for full-size (15 $\times$ 15 array) sensors, including leakage-current and breakdown measurements performed on all sensors at the vendor sites, as well as more detailed electrical characterizations at the participating ATLAS-HGTD institutes. In addition, the electrical characterization of full-size sensors after irradiation is reported.

title: Sub-electron noise with a buried-channel DePFET: characterisation of novel DePFET concepts
abstract: Depleted P-channel Field Effect Transistor (DePFET) pixel sensors combine Fano-limited energy resolution with fast, low-noise readout and are used in instruments ranging from particle tracking to X-ray astronomy. In this work, two novel DePFET technologies that address the two factors of the signal-to-noise ratio through fundamental changes to the intrinsic design are characterised: a buried-channel design aimed at reducing the limiting low-frequency noise by weakening the coupling between the channel and Si/SiO$_2$ interface traps, and a super-$g_q$ design intended to increase the charge gain by reducing the effective internal-gate capacitance. Their noise and energy resolution were mapped across the transistor bias space, over a wide temperature range (100-260 K) and for integration times of 0.4-9 $\mu$s (readout times of 2-19.2 $\mu$s per row), and compared with standard DePFETs as developed for the NewAthena Wide Field Imager (WFI). All three variants reach their lowest noise at about 155 K. The buried-channel device achieves an excellent equivalent noise charge (ENC) of 0.96 e$^-$ (at most 0.83 e$^-$ after subtracting the readout-electronics noise), demonstrating sub-electron noise over a complete 64$\times$64 DePFET matrix in a single readout, alongside a power consumption reduction of more than 50%. The super-$g_q$ DePFET shows a 2.6-fold increase in charge gain (about 1100 pA/e$^-$) but exhibits higher total noise due to an excess noise contribution. The results highlight the potential of the novel DePFETs, with the buried-channel technology offering immediate benefits for low-noise applications such as the WFI.

title: Cancellation of cryocooler-induced vibration in trapped-ion systems
abstract: Mechanical cryocoolers offer numerous benefits for the operation of vacuum systems containing trapped atomic ions. However, the fidelity of laser-based gates can be degraded by phase noise induced by the cryocooler vibrations. We present a feed-forward vibration-cancellation system that directly measures inner shield displacement with an auxiliary interferometer and applies a compensating phase correction to the laser drive. The interferometer signal is demodulated, and a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) system unwraps the displacement measurement signal, computes the required correction phase, and updates the RF drive of an in-line acousto-optic modulator (AOM) to correct for the vibration-induced dephasing. With cancellation active, the qubit coherence time improves from $3.0\pm0.4$ ms to $35\pm5$ ms, consistent with a simulation based on the measured vibration spectrum. We further validate the cancellation by artificially increasing the mechanical coupling of the cryocooler to the vacuum chamber. The vibration-induced decoherence rate is suppressed by a factor of approximately 70 at an RMS (root mean square) displacement of 0.65 $\mathrm{\mu}$m.
